report:
## Conclusion

The claim that **taking ibuprofen for COVID-19 worsens the infection is not supported by the available clinical evidence**.

The concern began early in 2020 after a hypothesis that NSAIDs might affect ACE2 (a receptor used by SARS‑CoV‑2) and warnings from a French official. This was biologically speculative—not evidence that ibuprofen caused worse outcomes in people.

Subsequent evidence has not found that association. A clinical study that followed COVID-19 patients for outcomes including severity, oxygen needs, hospitalization, and death found no signal that ibuprofen/NSAID use worsened outcomes. UK medicines regulators likewise concluded there was insufficient evidence that ibuprofen or other NSAIDs increase either susceptibility to COVID-19 or worsening of its symptoms. A Danish analysis also reported no scientific evidence that ibuprofen worsens COVID-19.

This does **not** mean ibuprofen is appropriate for everyone: it can cause kidney injury, stomach bleeding/ulcers, fluid retention, and drug interactions, particularly with dehydration, kidney disease, ulcers, anticoagulants, or some heart conditions. It also treats pain/fever; it is not an antiviral COVID-19 treatment. Follow the label and clinician advice, especially if you have risk factors.

- https://laegemiddelstyrelsen.dk/en/news/2020/new-data-analysis-ibuprofen-does-not-worsen-covid-19-infection
